passages.original: Nec negandum colobii aut dalmaticarum voces antiquas esse. In vita S. Cypriani a Pontio scripta legimus: I Et cum se dalmatica exspoliasset (Cyprianus), et diaconibus tradidisset, in linea stetit. » Antiquus auctor, Quæst. Vet. et Nov. Test. apud Augustinum , Append. t. III, c. 49, cum romanae ecclesire diaconis ita espostulat : « Quasi non hodie diaconi |dalmaticis induantur sicut episcopi. » tlhi et dalmaticarum usum episcoporum proprium esse, et a romanis diaconis per arrogantiam usurpatum esse not at. Scribit et Cyprianus tolonensis episcopus in Vita S. Cæsarii arelatensis episcopi, |eo ipso tempore, quo Symmachus papa Cæsarium « concesso specialiter pallii decoravit privilegio, diaconos quoque ipsius ad Romanæ instar ecclesiae dalmaticarum fecisse habitu præeminere.
passages.english: Nor should it be denied that the words *colobium* and *dalmatica* are ancient. In the Life of St. Cyprian written by Pontius we read: "And when he (Cyprian) had stripped off his dalmatic and handed it to the deacons, he stood in his linen [garment]." An ancient author, in the Questions on the Old and New Testament found among Augustine's works (Appendix, vol. III, ch. 49), complains thus against the deacons of the Roman church: "As if deacons today were not clothed in dalmatics just as bishops are." There he notes both that the use of dalmatics is proper to bishops and that it was usurped by the Roman deacons out of arrogance. Cyprian, bishop of Toulon, also writes in the Life of St. Caesarius, bishop of Arles, that at the very time when Pope Symmachus "adorned [Caesarius] with the privilege of the pallium, granted specially, he also caused his deacons, after the model of the Roman church, to be distinguished by the dress of dalmatics."
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'I Et' (opening quotation mark), 'ecclesire' for ecclesiae, 'espostulat' for expostulat, 'tlhi' for Ibi, 'not at' for notat; stray '|' marks omitted. The *colobium* was a sleeveless or short-sleeved tunic. The closing quotation is left open in the text and continues into the following context.
